Klawock|United States of America.f: The first cannery in Alaska opened here in 1878, built by a San Francisco firm.

Port Heiden|United States of America.f: It appeared in the 1880 census as the Aleut village of Mashikh, and was listed as Meshik in 1890 before becoming Port Heiden.

Platinum|United States of America.f: A Yup'ik prospector's 1926 find at Fox Gulch proved to be platinum, and in WWII it was the Western Hemisphere's only source of the metal.

Fort Yukon|United States of America.f: Alaska's all-time record high of 100 F was recorded here on June 27, 1915, in a village that straddles the Arctic Circle.

St. George Island|United States of Ameri.f: The island is the breeding site of over 75% of the known population of red-legged kittiwakes.

Carlsbad (CA)|United States of America.f: Settlers named it after Karlsbad in Bohemia because a local well's water was chemically similar to that of famed spas.

Anaktuvuk Pass|United States of America.f: The name comes from the Inupiaq anaqtugvik, meaning place of caribou droppings.

Cape Lisburne|United States of America.f: Cook left a blank for this cape's name in his 1778 journal, and someone else later wrote in Lisburne.

Emmonak|United States of America.f: Villagers moved to Emmonak in 1964 after flooding damaged old Kwiguk, one of the last settlements before the Yukon meets the Bering Sea.

Barter Island|United States of America.f: Until the late 1800s it was a major trade center where the Inupiat bartered with peoples from both Alaska and Canada.

Gambell|United States of America.f: Gambell lies 36 miles from Siberia, and in 1955 locals rescued the wounded crew of a US Navy plane attacked by Soviet fighters.

Arctic Village|United States of America.f: It recorded -13 F on September 30, 1970, the lowest temperature ever measured in Alaska in the month of September.

Wainwright|United States of America.f: It is named for Wainwright Lagoon, which honored Lt. John Wainwright of Captain Beechey's 1826 expedition.

Molokai|United States of America.f: Molokai has the highest sea cliffs in the world and the longest fringing reef in the U.S., nearly 25 miles long.

Savoonga|United States of America.f: It calls itself the Walrus Capital of the World, and reindeer brought to the island in 1900 numbered over 10,000 by 1917.

Atqasuk|United States of America.f: Atqasuk means downslope in Inupiaq, and a WWII coal mine nearby supplied fuel to facilities in Utqiagvik.

Nuiqsut|United States of America.f: Families who resettled the village in the early 1970s lived in tents for a year while housing was built.

Michigan City|United States of America.f: The sand on the beaches in and near the city is nicknamed singing sand because of the sound it produces.

Ocean City|United States of America.f: Its inlet was carved by a hurricane in August 1933, which also destroyed the railroad tracks across Sinepuxent Bay.

Westerly|United States of America.f: Westerly is a tourist destination from May through October, when its population nearly doubles.

Ambler|United States of America.f: A Kobuk River tributary honors Dr. James Ambler, who starved after his ship was trapped in Arctic ice in 1881, and the town took its name.

Holy Cross|United States of America.f: It showed up in the 1880 census as Askhomute, then as Kozerevsky and Koserefsky, before settling on the name Holy Cross.

Huslia|United States of America.f: In January 2025 Huslia was 20 F warmer than usual, the largest heat increase in the country that month.

Haines|United States of America.f: Haines is the only town in Southeast Alaska named for a woman, Francina Haines, who chaired fundraising for its 1881 mission.

Kiana|United States of America.f: A weak tornado touched down here on August 26, 1976, the northernmost tornado on record.

Anvik|United States of America.f: Anvik means exit in Central Yup'ik, and a national side trail links it to the Iditarod Trail 86 miles to the east.

Ruby|United States of America.f: The largest gold nugget ever found in Alaska, 294.10 troy ounces, was found near Ruby in 1998.

Sand Point|United States of America.f: Founded by a San Francisco fishing company in 1898 as a cod station, it is now home to the Aleutians' largest fishing fleet.

Hana|United States of America.f: Queen Kaahumanu was born in Hana in 1768, and Charles Lindbergh was buried near the town in 1974.

Point Lay|United States of America.f: Its Inupiaq name Kali means mound, after a raised area on the barrier island where the old village stood.

Friday Harbor|United States of America.f: Named for Joseph Friday, a Native Hawaiian shepherd, it is where Osamu Shimomura harvested jellyfish for green fluorescent protein.

Deering|United States of America.f: Its name probably comes from the schooner Abbie M. Deering, which Kipling mentions in Captains Courageous.

Mekoryuk|United States of America.f: In 1934, 34 musk oxen from Greenland were moved to Nunivak Island to save the species, and the herd now numbers around 500.

Newport|United States of America.f: Touro Synagogue, the oldest existing synagogue in the United States, stands here, and the Newport Jazz Festival began here in 1954.

Orcas Island|United States of America.f: Orcas is short for Horcasitas, the name of a Spanish colonial official, and Mount Constitution is the highest point in the San Juans.

Aleknagik|United States of America.f: The name comes from a Yupik phrase meaning wrong way home, for travelers lost in fog who ended up in the lake instead.

Ironwood|United States of America.f: A 52-foot fiberglass statue of Hiawatha, billed as the World's Tallest Indian, stands here.

St Mary's (AK)|United States of America.f: The neighboring village of Andreafsky, once called Clear River, merged into St. Mary's in 1980.

Martha's Vineyard|United States of Ameri.f: By the late 19th century, one in 155 islanders was born deaf, about 37 times the national rate.
